extracted.intended_audience: general readers and publishing professionals (authors, publishers, judges) seeking information about the Booker Prize
extracted.subtask_description: Rules, eligibility, nomination and judging procedures for the Booker Prize (with notes on related prizes). Covers language and publication requirements, who may submit, judge composition and the longlist/shortlist/winner selection process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Award purpose / scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Awarded for Best work of sustained fiction of the year, written in English and published in the UK or Ireland.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prize is conferred each year for a single work of sustained fiction written in English and published in the United Kingdom or Ireland. It is regarded as a prestigious literary award; the winner receives £50,000 and international publicity that usually leads to a significant sales boost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Work must be written in English (English-language novels are eligible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since 2014 eligibility was widened to any English-language novel (regardless of the author's nationality) so long as it is published in the UK or Ireland; this change was controversial in literary circles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication geography requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligible works must be published in the United Kingdom or Ireland.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irrespective of the author's nationality (after 2014), the work must have been published in the UK or Ireland to be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form requirement — single work of sustained fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The prize is for a single work of sustained fiction; short story collections are not eligible for the Booker Prize (though they may be eligible for the International Booker).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Booker Prize is for a single work of sustained fiction in English; note the International Booker Prize (separate) does allow short story collections and is awarded for translated works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical nationality eligibility (pre-2014)
rubrics_metrics.description: Originally only novels written by Commonwealth, Irish and South African (later Zimbabwean) citizens were eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This historical restriction was lifted in 2014 to allow any English-language novel published in the UK or Ireland; the change provoked debate about the prize's identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge panel composition and appointment
rubrics_metrics.description: A five-person panel consisting of authors, publishers and journalists, as well as politicians, actors, artists and musicians, is appointed by the Booker Prize Foundation each year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gaby Wood (chief executive) chooses judges in consultation with an advisory committee of senior figures from the UK publishing industry. Judges are selected from among leading literary critics, writers, academics, and public figures; on rare occasions a judge may be selected a second time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge reading expectation / workload
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike some other literary prizes, each judge is expected to read all of the books that have been submitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges read all submitted books (example: in 2023 judges read 163 books over seven months). The expectation of reading every entry underpins the selection process and is often cited in critiques of the feasibility of a 'best book' chosen by a small panel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection process and reading rounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection proceeds by forming a longlist, then a shortlist, then choosing a winner, with multiple readings at each stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges select a longlist of 12 or 13 titles (the 'Booker Dozen'), then each reads those longlisted books a second time; from these they select a shortlist of six titles and read the six books a third time before selecting a winner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longlist and shortlist sizes (procedural constraint)
rubrics_metrics.description: Longlist of 12 or 13 titles (the 'Booker Dozen'); shortlist of six titles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From 2001 the longlist began to be published annually; since 2007 the number of nominees has been capped at 12 or 13 each year. The shortlist is then reduced to six titles for final consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission quota per publisher / imprint
rubrics_metrics.description: Each publisher's imprint may submit a number of titles based on their longlisting history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-longlisted publishers can submit one title; publishers with one or two longlisted books in the previous five years can submit two; those with three or four longlisted books are allowed three submissions; publishers with five or more longlisted books can have four submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatic consideration of previous winners
rubrics_metrics.description: Previous winners of the prize are automatically considered if they enter new titles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Past winners may enter new books and will be considered automatically (in addition to regular submission rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Call-in / written representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Books may be called in to the judges: publishers can make written representations to request consideration of titles in addition to those entered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a route for publishers to ask the judges to consider titles beyond the standard submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule on single winner (award-splitting)
rubrics_metrics.description: A rule established in 1993 made it mandatory for the appointed jury to make the award to a single author/book (i.e., not split).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite the rule, in 2019 the foundation's jury split the prize between two authors in breach of that rule, a decision that generated controversy and commentary about jury discretion versus formal rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prize money and distribution to shortlisted authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Winner receives £50,000; each shortlisted author receives £2,500 and a specially bound edition of their book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prize money has changed over time (originally £5,000, doubled in 1978, raised to £50,000 in 2002). The winner's reward includes public recognition and sales impact; for related prizes (e.g., International Booker) the £50,000 is split between author and translator.

rubrics_metrics.name: International Booker Prize criteria (related award)
rubrics_metrics.description: The International Booker Prize is awarded for a work of fiction translated into English and published in the United Kingdom or Ireland; short story collections are eligible for the International Booker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since 2016 the International Booker is given annually to a single book in English translation, with a £50,000 prize shared equally between author and translator. It is distinct from the Booker Prize for single works written in English.

rubrics_metrics.name: Children's Booker Prize criteria (related award)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Children's Booker Prize (announced 2025) is for the best contemporary fiction for children aged 8–12.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by AKO Foundation, inaugural award to be presented in 2027; includes young judges and a jury chaired by Frank Cottrell-Boyce (as of the announcement). This is a separate prize with its own age/genre eligibility.
